A content delivery network is a system of computer servers spread across many cities and countries, all storing copies of the same website content so that no single machine has to handle every request alone. The original copy of a website lives on one machine called the origin server, which acts as the master source of truth. Because visiting that one server from far away can be slow, copies of the content get placed on servers closer to people, called edge locations, positioned nearer to homes, offices, and phones around the world. When a request for a page arrives, the network checks whether a nearby edge location already has a saved copy; if it does, that's called a cache hit, and the content gets delivered almost instantly without bothering the distant original at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that all keep copies of the same popular book, so nobody has to travel across the country to the one main archive every time they want to read it. Only when a nearby library lacks a copy does someone fetch it from the archive, and afterward that library keeps a copy for next time. This arrangement makes websites load faster, keeps them running even during traffic surges, and reduces strain on the original server.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The one original computer holding the real, master version of a website | Everything else is copied from here, so it must stay reliable |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a saved copy of content | Being physically closer means faster delivery to nearby visitors |
| Cache hit | A moment when a nearby copy is found and used instead of the original | Saves time and avoids overloading the origin server |
| Content delivery network | The whole system of connected copy-holding servers working together | Makes websites feel fast and stay available everywhere |
